questions.q: Why does this lesson describe solution architecture as a cross-cutting practice rather than a sixth domain alongside data, integration, identity, security, and delivery?
options: Because it's the discipline of balancing trade-offs across all five domains for one specific solution, rather than being its own isolated body of knowledge
Because it's actually identical to security architecture
Because it only applies to projects with no security requirements
Because Salesforce does not recognize solution architecture as a real role
questions.explain: Solution architecture doesn't have its own separate technical subject matter the way data or security architecture does — it's the practice of finding a design that balances all the other domains together for one real solution.

questions.q: In the distributor-order worked example, what would data architecture prefer if optimizing purely for its own domain?
options: A fully deferred rollout with no object created yet
Named Salesforce logins for every distributor
A heavily sandboxed integration path that never touches core objects
A dedicated Distributor Order object, cleanly separated from internal Opportunities, with its own tailored fields
questions.explain: Data architecture optimizing in isolation would favor the cleanest possible object model for this specific use case — a dedicated object tailored to distributor orders, separate from Opportunities.

questions.q: Why don't the five domain-optimal answers in the distributor-order example automatically combine into one coherent solution?
options: Because they actually already agree perfectly with no conflict
Because Salesforce technically forbids combining more than two domains in one design

Because each domain's ideal choice can directly conflict with another's — e.g., full named distributor logins (identity's preference) conflicts with heavily sandboxed isolation (security's preference)
Because only one domain's answer is ever allowed to be used
questions.explain: Each domain's isolated preference is individually defensible, but they pull in different directions — identity wants flexible named access, security wants tight isolation, data wants a clean dedicated model that may not fit a batch sync cadence, and delivery wants to defer for safety.

questions.q: What is the central point this lesson makes about finding the "best" answer in each domain and stapling them together?
options: That approach always produces the ideal solution-level design

Solution architecture isn't about independently finding each domain's best answer and combining them — it's about finding a combination that's genuinely good enough across all domains together, even if not optimal in any single one
Only the security domain's answer should ever be used, regardless of other domains
Domain-level optimization is irrelevant and should never be considered at all
questions.explain: A solution architect's job is to find a design that works end to end across every domain, which often means each domain gives up a bit of its own ideal outcome in exchange for a solution that's actually buildable, secure, and usable as a whole.

questions.q: What did this lesson's proposed resolved design for the distributor-order scenario land on, as an example of a solution-level compromise?
options: A dedicated lightweight object fed via moderate-frequency batch sync, accessed through a tightly scoped integration rather than full logins, with a phased pilot rollout
Full named Salesforce logins for every distributor with real-time sync and no phased rollout
Canceling the project entirely since no domain could agree
Giving every distributor full administrator access to simplify the integration
questions.explain: The proposed compromise took a bit from each domain's instinct — a dedicated but lightweight object, a batch sync rather than real-time, scoped rather than full access, and a phased rollout — rather than fully satisfying any one domain's isolated ideal.
